items.caption:
Tiny job, tiny budget: take it or pass? Run this check first (save it).

"It's only 10 minutes for you" is never 10 minutes. A brief, a call, the edit, two rounds of changes, the invoice, the chasing.

Set a minimum fee:
1. Your hourly rate (say $40)
2. × the hours ANY job costs you, however small (say 6)
3. = $240. Round up: $250.

Then ask 4 questions:
• Does it pay my minimum?
• Is the scope written down?
• Is there real work after it?
• Does it fit without bumping a bigger client?

Mostly no? Pass, or offer less scope for your minimum. Hold the price, flex the scope.

Send this to a freelancer who says yes to every "quick" job.

items.caption:
Rule 3 is the one nobody follows. 3 rules for on-screen text that people actually read:

1. Top half. Text low on the screen gets covered by your caption and the buttons. Move it up.
2. One read. If it needs two reads, it's too long. Keep each screen under 10 words.
3. New scene, new text. The same line sitting there for 10 seconds feels frozen. Change it when the scene changes so sound-off viewers see the story move.

Save this for your next edit, and send it to the friend whose text hides behind the buttons.
